entries.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
entries.summary: Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.
entries.content:
Europe

Russia's new suspected radar in Kaliningrad could spy deep into Europe

November 1, 2026

Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as  right across Ukraine.

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.

Mass surveillance system

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

Electronic warfare hub

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

Motivation for the West

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

entries.title: Serbia: Police chief arrested after election for abuse of office
entries.summary: Marko Kricak, an Aleksandar Vucic loyalist, is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into a gangland murder. Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election defeat.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia: Police chief arrested after election for abuse of office

November 1, 2026

Marko Kricak, an Aleksandar Vucic loyalist, is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into a gangland murder. Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election defeat.

The head of Serbia's criminal police directorate has been arrested and charged with abuse of office, state media reported on Sunday.

Marko Kricak is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into the murder in May of a suspected criminal underworld figure in a Belgrade restaurant.

Serbia: who is police chief Marko Kricak?

The 42-year-old was seen as a supporter of defeated Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, whose right-wing populist camp was defeated by the opposition Student List in parliamentary elections on October 25.

Indeed, he has also been accused by student groups of "brutality" in the police response to peaceful anti-Vucic demonstrations.

The removal of Kricak and other Vucic loyalists in Serbia's police and intelligence apparatus was one of student leaders' demands.

But Belgrade's chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, denied a connection between the student movement's demands and Kricak's arrest.

"This arrest has no link with ... the result of the legislative elections," he told journalists.

Serbia: Vucic system dismantled

Nevertheless, the arrest of a senior police officer regarded as close to the former regime is being seen as an example of the strongholds of the Vucic system slowly eroding.

Kricak worked as a car salesman before being recruited into Serbia's domestic intelligence agency, the BIA, and was a loyal supporter of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

In July 2023, he was appointed commander of the Serbian police's personal protection unit (JZO).

It was in this position that he is alleged to have personally led the abduction of a group of university students, allegedly assaulting one female student and threatening to rape her in the basement of a government building in Belgrade.

At the end of 2025, he was appointed head of the Serbian Criminal Police.

entries.title: France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack
entries.summary: Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous weekends.
entries.content:
France

France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack

November 1, 2026

Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous weekends.

Paris prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation Sunday after a Molotov cocktail was thrown at security forces during a demonstration in the French capital.

Prosecutors said explosive projectiles targeted about 15 gendarmes as well as police officers. No suspects have been arrested over the attack, and investigators were still establishing the number and severity of injuries.

What happened in Paris?

The attack took place at Porte de Charenton, where Saturday's march ended. Photographs and video from the AFP news agency showed an incendiary device exploding at a gendarme's feet and setting his protective equipment alight.

Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, although those details remained provisional. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described the attack as an attempted murder.

How many people were arrested?

The Interior Ministry reported 779 arrests nationwide during the demonstrations and Halloween night. The figure includes both events, updating Saturday evening's provisional total of 565. Authorities said the later part of the night passed without major incidents.

Paris prosecutors separately reported 105 arrests in the capital: 88 linked to the demonstrations and 17 to Halloween night. They said 89 people remained in custody, including at least 22 minors.

The protests focused on high living costs and government policies. The ministry put nationwide turnout at 320,000, while unions estimated nearly 500,000 participants.

The nationwide arrest total was below the 1,314 recorded during the previous Saturday's mobilization and the 2,628 on October 17, when widespread rioting and looting broke out. Authorities had increased security ahead of Halloween amid online calls for violence.

entries.title: Ukraine news: Oleshky ceasefire ends as Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
entries.summary: A US-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region ended on Sunday night with no violations reported. Elsewhere, however, Russia struck energy infrastructure in at least four other regions. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Oleshky ceasefire ends, Russian attacks continue

Published October 31, 2026last updated November 1, 2026

A US-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region ended on Sunday night with no violations reported. Elsewhere, however, Russia struck energy infrastructure in at least four other regions. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Localized Oleshy ceasefire ended at 11 p.m. local time (10 p.m. CET)

  • Oleshky evacuees arrive in Ukrainian territory from Belarus

  • Russian strikes leave tens of thousands across Ukraine without power, including in the capital Kyiv

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says preparations for talks with US and Russia underway after meeting with Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan

Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1:

Skip next section Kherson: 167 more people evacuated as end of ceasefire draws near

Kherson: 167 more people evacuated as end of ceasefire draws near

The Ukrainian military evacuated a further 167 civilians from the partially occupied southern region of Kherson on Sunday, the army's general staff confirmed shortly before a localized six-day ceasefire was due to expire.

Among the evacuees were 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility, according to the announcement.

The temporary truce in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to expire at 11 p.m. local time (10 p.m. CET).

Local governor Olexander Prokudin called on residents in the region to remain alert and warned people not to enter or approach areas close to the Dnipro river which flows through Kherson.

Ukrainian officials said the intensity of Russian drone and artillery strikes remained high in those areas.

Skip next section Russia refused to extend Kherson ceasefire, Ukrainian official says

Russia refused to extend Kherson ceasefire, Ukrainian official says

Ukraine offered to extend the US-brokered ceasefire for the Kherson region but Russia refused, a senior Ukrainian official told the AFP news agency.

The truce, which only applied to the southeastern region of Kherson, expires at 10:59 p.m. local time (2059 GMT) on Sunday evening.

The official told AFP that the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry had made the offer but "the Russians don't want to."

The ceasefire, which the White House says was brokered by First Lady Melania Trump, began on Tuesday and has allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

Around 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the ceasefire took effect this week. They were given the choice of leaving the area to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or of staying in the city, which has been resupplied during the truce.

US President Donald Trump called for the ceasefire to become the "starting point for lasting peace."

"The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace."

Skip next section Russian drone attacks in central Ukraine kills three, injures 4

Russian drone attacks in central Ukraine kills three, injures 4

A Russian drone attack on Koziatyn in central Ukraine has killed at least three people and injured four others, including three children, local authorities said Sunday.

Vinnytsia regional military administrator Nataliya Zabolotna said on Facebook that a 13-year-old girl was among those who died.

"Two five-year-old children and a 16-year-old boy" sustained injuries, she said, as well as a 24-year-old man.

The victims were injured when a drone exploded between a residential building and a school, officials said.

Russian drone strikes were also reported in the western region of Chernivtsi. One person was injured and an administrative building was severely damaged, regional military administrator Ruslan Osypenko said.

Skip next section WATCH: European ministers shun Russia at G20

WATCH: European ministers shun Russia at G20

Foreign ministers from countries making up the G20 refused to take part in the traditional group photo with Russia's Sergey Lavrov.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio canceled the event because of the boycott, as Russia's war in Ukraine and Moscow's diplomatic isolation from many Western countries overshadowed the summit.

Skip next section WATCH: Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation

WATCH: Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation

Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky have arrived in Ukrainian-held territory after a rare localized ceasefire enabled civilians to leave.

Speaking to DW, evacuees described years of isolation, food shortages, and regular shelling, with some saying they survived by eating grass and dogs as supplies ran out.

The rescue operation brought families back together at a reception point in northern Ukraine, where relatives, volunteers, and local residents welcomed the arrivals after their journey through Russia and Belarus.

Skip next section Preparations for trilateral talks underway, Zelenskyy says after Erdogan meeting

Preparations for trilateral talks underway, Zelenskyy says after Erdogan meeting

Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on Saturday evening for talks that the Ukrainian president said included preparations for a three-way summit between Ukraine, Russia and the United States.

He said the meeting would be held in the first half of November.

"President Erdogan and I discussed the prospects for this format and other possibilities, including ways to involve Turkey and all of Europe, as well as the possibility of holding meetings here in Turkey," Zelenskyy said.

"At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish."

Previous rounds of talks between Ukraine and Russia brokered by Turkey failed to yield a lasting peace agreement.

Describing the meetings as "important and substantive," Zelenskyy said he and Erdogan had also discussed security issues concerning shipping through the Black Sea.

"This includes food security, and today President Erdogan and I agreed to work on a Black Sea grain corridor to ensure that the corridor exists and operates effectively," the Ukrainian leader told a press conference.

Skip next section Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire for Kherson set to expire

Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire for Kherson set to expire

A ceasefire limited to the Kherson region in eastern Ukraine that was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump was set to expire on Sunday evening, after neither Russia nor Ukraine announced an extension.

The rare truce, which began on Tuesday, is the longest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The ceasefire allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

While neither side reported violations of the ceasefire, Russian strikes continued overnight, with fresh power outages reported across Ukraine on Sunday, its energy ministry and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian strikes on the Russian-occupied region of Luhansk killed at least four people since Sunday evening, Russian-backed local authorities said.

Skip next section Russian strikes leave vast numbers of Ukrainian homes without power

Russian strikes leave vast numbers of Ukrainian homes without power

Hundreds of thousands of households lost electricity after overnight Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.

In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said energy infrastructure in four regions — Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi — had been struck.

"Substations, transformers, and power lines that supply electricity to our people's homes were targeted. Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He added that "massive Russian attacks on Ukraine's other critical infrastructure are also continuing unabated."

"The intensity of the strikes is very high," he said, accusing Russia of seeking to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy repeated his call to the US, Europe and Ukraine's other partners to do more to deliver missiles and other weaponry to better defend against the Russian attacks.

"These deliveries cannot take years. Russia is destroying infrastructure and killing our people right now, and it is betting on ballistic missiles this winter. Accordingly, decisions on air defense must also be implemented now," the Ukrainian president said.

Skip next section Kremlin wants initial Ukraine talks without Europe

Kremlin wants initial Ukraine talks without Europe

Russia wants the opening rounds of renewed peace negotiations to involve only Moscow, Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.

Asked whether European countries should participate, Ushakov pointed to Russia's existing contacts with the United States.

"We have working contacts with the Americans," Interfax quoted him as saying. It was therefore "logical" for at least the first rounds to take place in a trilateral format, he added.

Skip next section Russia reports major damage after drone attack near refinery

Russia reports major damage after drone attack near refinery

A drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility east of Moscow, a Russian governor said, following Ukrainian reports of a strike on a major oil refinery.

Nizhny Novgorod Governor Gleb Nikitin reported a "massive drone attack" overnight, saying more than 100 drones were destroyed. Preliminary information indicated no casualties, he added.

Nikitin did not identify the damaged facility. Ukrainian media reported that the target was the Kstovo oil refinery, describing it as one of Russia's largest.

The reports could not be independently verified.

Authorities said they were taking steps to keep fuel available at gas stations.

Russia said Ukraine had resumed attacks on its refineries after a pause. US President Donald Trump had pressured Kyiv to stop such strikes, blaming them for rising diesel prices.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil and gas facilities in response to Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.

Skip next section Welcome back to our live coverage

Welcome back to our live coverage

Welcome back to our coverage. Follow the latest developments throughout the day.

Skip next section We're pausing the blog for today

We're pausing the blog for today

Thank you for joining today. We'll be back with the latest developments on Sunday.

Skip next section IN PHOTOS: Evacuees reunite with family after fleeing Oleshky

IN PHOTOS: Evacuees reunite with family after fleeing Oleshky

Ukraine spent months demanding that Russia allow people to evacuate out of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, after food delivery supplies stopped earlier this year.

Hundreds of people made their way out on Saturday.

Skip next section Wadephul says Europe and US are 'on the same side' on Russia

Wadephul says Europe and US are 'on the same side' on Russia

At a news conference after the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez Gruber asked German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul whether Sergey Lavrov's presence and the possibility of Russian President Vladimir Putin attending the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, in December signaled a normalization of relations with Russia.

Wadephul said the US and European countries were "on the same side."

"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," he said, adding that foreign ministers must be prepared to engage even with adversaries.

"You don't have to negotiate with partners, but you have to negotiate with somebody who has a different position and who's somehow also an adversary to freedom and to security in Europe. So it is necessary that we speak, and for that reason I think it was useful," Wadephul added.

The G20 foreign ministers skipped their traditional family photo at a meeting in Atlanta on Friday, amid objections from several European countries, Australia and Canada to appearing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

Wadephul said: "We are not in a position that it was necessary or useful or a good idea to have a family photo because in the very situation we are in, Russia does not really show an interest to share our values and to share our interests."

The US State Department removed the photo from the agenda to prevent it from becoming a distraction or a spectacle.

Skip next section Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks on Black Sea shipping

Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks on Black Sea shipping

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Istanbul for talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, with Black Sea shipping among the issues on the agenda.

"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Türkiye, and real diplomatic prospects," Zelenskyy wrote on X, using the alternative spelling for Turkey.

The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.

entries.title: Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union
entries.summary: Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.
entries.content:
Kazakhstan

Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union

November 1, 2026

Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.

She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.

"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.

Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.

Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.

From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.

But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalinstarted deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.

Collective punishment

Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.

There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.

"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."

Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."

Culture and remembrance under one roof

The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.

Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.

During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.

The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.

Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.

Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.

Representative stories

One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."

She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.

Karlag was by far the biggest camp system and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.

Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.

Staged remembrance

The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.

Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."

Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.

"The landscape has been shaped by forced labor"

"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.

"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.

The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.

Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.

The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."

This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

entries.title: Germany news: Gen Z group calls for new protests
entries.summary: The group behind German demonstrations this weekend has called for more protests to keep pressure on the government to act. Meanwhile, the IG Metall union has begun warning strikes after pay talks collapse. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Gen Z group calls for new protests

Published October 31, 2026last updated November 1, 2026

The group behind German demonstrations this weekend has called for more protests to keep pressure on the government to act. Meanwhile, the IG Metall union has begun warning strikes after pay talks collapse. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Gen Z regelt says it had no influence on violent looting after its protests ended
  • German Interior Minister Dobrindt blames left, migrant 'troublemakers' for violence
  • Former Chancellor Angela Merkel calls for Germany's first female president
  • Berlin's Left Party voted in favor of coalition talks with the Social Democrats and Greens, talks could start Monday

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of October 31 - November 1, 2026:

Skip next section Children across Germany find needles in Halloween candy

Children across Germany find needles in Halloween candy

Needles or other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets children collected while trick-or-treating for Halloween, German police said Sunday.

Police believe most or all of the objects, which also included metal screws, were placed intentionally to cause harm.

Incidents were reported in Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, and Rhineland-Palatinate, among other locations, police said.

In one of the cases in the southern city of Nuremberg, police said a child had bitten down on a needle while eating a piece of chocolate. The child was unharmed.

In two separate cases in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, police said the needles had been concealed as such that they were not visible from the outside.

In several of the cases, police have opened investigations into attempted aggravated assault.

No suspects have been identified.

Skip next section Natural gas supply is secure as Germany misses storage target, ministry says

Natural gas supply is secure as Germany misses storage target, ministry says

Despite the country's natural gas storage facilities being at about 61.2% capacity, Germany's supply is secure, according to the Economy Ministry.

"Germany's gas supply is secure for the coming winter, even with the current storage levels," a spokeswoman for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said.

Average storage levels were supposed to reach 70% by Sunday.

"Based on the current assessment, we expect Germany to get through the winter in good shape. Security of supply depends not only on storage levels, but also on actual gas withdrawals, ongoing gas imports and additional precautionary measures," the spokeswoman added.

The Federal Network Agency also said the country's gas supply remained stable.

"Security of supply is guaranteed," it said. "Based on the information currently available, the Federal Network Agency continues to consider the risk of stressed gas supply to be low."

Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of the Initiative Energien Speichern (Energy Storage Initiative), told the German dpa news agency that failure to meet storage targets was a "serious warning."

"Germany is entering the heating season with smaller safety reserves. This increases the vulnerability of the gas supply, particularly in the event of exceptionally low temperatures or additional disruptions to gas imports," Heinermann said.

Skip next section Over 100 officers injured in Frankfurt, 54 people taken into custody

Over 100 officers injured in Frankfurt, 54 people taken into custody

More than 100 officers were injured, one of them seriously, during violent confrontations in Frankfurt after largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday, according to Roman Poseck, the interior minister in the state of Hesse, where Frankfurt is located.

He added that up to 1,300 officers were on duty in Frankfurt on Saturday night and into Sunday morning.

The minister said 17 stores were damaged and five were looted. Police took 54 people into custody, all between the ages of 13 and 29.

Of the more than 8,000 people who took part in the protests in Frankfurt, authorities estimated there were 1,000 to 1,500 violent troublemakers, "predominantly from a migrant background."

Poseck said, "An enormous potential for violence on the part of left-wing extremists and violence-prone young people, mostly from migrant backgrounds, has been unleashed."

"This group of offenders was predominantly made up of migrants. And we must address that too," he added. "There must be no false taboos here."

After blaming migrants for the violence, Poseck said German citizens made up the vast majority of those detained.

In Cologne, which also saw violent confrontations between rioters and police, state Interior Minister Herbert Reul said left-wing extremists hijacked the Gen Z protests.

"Anyone who throws rocks and firecrackers at police officers, sets off fireworks, and rampages through the streets has no political agenda," Reul said in a statement. "People who cover their faces don't want to discuss or persuade. They want trouble and violence. There’s no justification for that."

Skip next section Europe needs to close AI gap with US, China, German president says

Europe needs to close AI gap with US, China, German president says

Despite considerable attention given to regulating artificial intelligence, European countries need to do more to understand how AI is applied and to keep up with advances made in China and the United States, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD.

"We can only have a serious say in the regulatory framework — an international regulatory framework — if we actually understand the conditions under which it is applied," Steinmeier said, according to remarks released ahead of the broadcast of ARD's Sunday evening interview program. "In that respect, I believe Europe does not have the option of saying no to AI."

He said how countries decide to use and regulate AI could "be a matter of European security."

"But above all, it is also an ethical question of where the limits of our ability to control this technology actually lie," Steinmeier said.

Steinmeier, who is finishing his second and final term in office, wrapped up a multi-day tour of China on Saturday. Germany is currently debating who could succeed him. 

Skip next section German Gen Z group calls for more demonstrations

German Gen Z group calls for more demonstrations

The group that organized this weekend's protests, "Gen Z regelt" roughly "Gen Z takes charge," distanced itself from violent riots that occurred after the rallies and called for new demonstrations later this month.

The initiative's organizers issued a positive assessment of protests across Germany.

"Today, 100,000 people showed why they're taking to the streets," a spokesperson for the initiative said Saturday, adding that estimates of participation in six to eight cities would come later.

Gen Z regelt planned protests in 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich, and has called for people to take to the streets again on November 14.

The group has called for more funding for schools, addiction treatment, and psychotherapy as well as measures to combat rising living costs. While it promotes social justice and greater climate protection, it opposes the introduction of mandatory military service, as well as an expansion of government surveillance.

"We are here ‌today ​to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion," Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said Saturday in Berlin. "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."

Gen Z regelt distanced itself from the violent riots and looting that followed the protests in some cities.

"We did not have any influence on what happened after the demonstrations," the group's spokesperson said.

Police also confirmed the demonstrations themselves were largely peaceful and that looting and riots afterward were set off by extremists using the protests for cover.

"The Gen Z protests turned out to be very peaceful," Andreas Rosskopf, chairman of the police union representing the Federal Police, told the Rheinische Post. He added that the groups responsible for the violence consisted of "autonomous and, in some cases, masked individuals."

In Cologne, which also saw looting, a police spokeswoman said the incidents were more likely linked to Halloween celebrations than to the aftermath of the Gen Z protests.

Skip next section People in Germany buying more organic food

People in Germany buying more organic food

Consumers in Germany bought more organic food products through the summer, with overall sales rising 2.8% to €4.42 billion ($4.95 billion) between July and September.

The German Federation of Organic Food Producers (BÖLW) reported that organic products' share of the German food market reached a record 8.1% in the third quarter.

"The growing organic market is a wake-up call," BÖLW head Tina Andres said, adding that many consumers see the organic sector as producing food locally and protecting water resources, insects and birds.

Supermarkets and discount retailers accounted for the largest share of third-quarter sales for organically produced food, at 31.3% and 27.8%, respectively. Drug store chains followed in third place with a market share of 12.7%. Specialty organic food retailers saw a 2.0% decline in sales, with a 17.3% market share.

Demand for organic products, which generally cost slightly more than traditionally produced products, has continued to grow steadily in Germany, except for a slowdown in 2022 caused by exceptionally high inflation at the time.

Skip next section Interior minister blames left, migrant 'troublemakers' for post-protest violence

Interior minister blames left, migrant 'troublemakers' for post-protest violence

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt condemned the riots that followed demonstrations in several major cities, including Berlin, Cologne and Frankfurt, blaming troublemakers for the violence and calling for severe criminal punishment of looters.

"Violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities in the evening hijacked the peaceful demonstrations that took place," he told the mass-market Bild newspaper on Sunday without elaborating on the identities of those taken into custody.

"The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable," he added. "Serious penalties must follow these breaches of the public peace."

Dobrindt said German police prevented widespread violence, such as that seen during protests in parts of some French cities.

"Excesses of violence like those seen in Paris were prevented thanks to the highly committed efforts of our police officers," said Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union. "The police operation strategy, involving a strong visible presence and the decentralized deployment of forces, proved successful."

Following peaceful demonstrations involving over 100,000 mainly young people, violent incidents and riots broke out after dark, particularly in Frankfurt and Cologne.

In France, protests ​continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 left significant damage to shops, public buildings and businesses.

Skip next section Police sent to protect vandalized shops in Frankfurt

Police sent to protect vandalized shops in Frankfurt

Police were patrolling the streets of downtown Frankfurt on Sunday morning, following looting that saw shop windows smashed and what a police spokesperson said was "considerable" damage to property.

The unrest followed demonstrations by young people demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice. Though the protests were largely peaceful, there were incidents of violence and rioting in Frankfurt and some other big German cities.

In Frankfurt, rioters smashed shop windows, stole goods from shops and attacked police officers. More than 30 people were detained and officers cordoned off parts of the city center. It was not immediately clear how many people were injured in the protests.

The police spokesperson said shops that were looted during the unrest also needed protection.

Hesse's state Premier Boris Rhein said he was shocked "by the violent excesses in Frankfurt," which "will not remain without consequences."

"Anyone who behaves like the attackers in Frankfurt's city center places themselves outside our society," Rhein said. "We will carefully assess the aggressors, perpetrator groups and the course of events, and draw our conclusions."

The group that organized the protests, "Gen Z regelt" roughly "Gen Z takes charge," had explicitly called for peaceful protests. German media in several cities observed extremists mixing into crowds of peaceful protesters.  

Skip next section IG Metall union begins warning strikes after pay talks collapse

IG Metall union begins warning strikes after pay talks collapse

Germany's IG Metall union began limited "warning strikes" in the metalworking and electrical sectors at midnight on Sunday.

The strikes began with about 300 night-shift employees at a factory in the western German state of Rhineland-Palatinate holding a rally outside the facility's entrance. A protest also began overnight at the mobile communications supplier RF 360 Europe/Qualcomm in Munich.

The warning strikes are set to spread across Germany next week. IG Metall is Germany's largest union and represents about 3.7 million workers in industrial sectors such as automotive manufacturing, mechanical engineering, electronics, and metal production.

The union has demanded a 5% pay increase over 12 months, as well as job and plant security.

In the second round of negotiations, employers presented an offer that included a one-time payment next year and a 1.3% step increase in July 2028, saying industry faced high cost burdens operating in Germany.

Union Chair Christiane Benner announced "major warning strikes" because the "so-called offer" met only with "incomprehension" in the workplaces, as the pay increases were well below the rate of inflation in Germany. 

Skip next section Berlin's Left Party votes in favor of coalition talks with Greens, SPD

Berlin's Left Party votes in favor of coalition talks with Greens, SPD

The Left Party in Berlin overwhelmingly voted in favor of formal talks to form a three-party coalition government with the Greens and Social Democrats.

Negotiations could begin on Monday as the Greens and SPD both already agreed to open formal talks for a government led by The Left in the city-state.

"We will not let ourselves be ground down, and I will not give up," Elif Eralp, The Left's parliamentary group leader, told party members during a congress on Saturday. She aims to be Berlin's first governing mayor from her party.

"Not a day passes without someone trying to force us and me to give up," she said, accusing Chancellor Friedrich Merz of trying to "blackmail" the Greens and SPD into abandoning plans for a coalition.

The Left emerged as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote in the state elections on September 20. Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) followed with 18.8%, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) with 16.3%, the Greens with 14.3% and the SPD with 12.1%. 

"The people of this city voted for us for change, and we will implement it," Eralp said. "They rightly expect us to pull every lever to improve their lives."

The three parties are expected to base their coalition negotiations on a preliminary agreement presented two weeks ago.

Its most controversial proposal would see around 160,000 flats owned by five major property companies transferred into public ownership in exchange for compensation.

Ahead of Saturday's vote, Berlin's Left Party has been dogged by allegations of antisemitism as well as a debate over Eralp's independence and ability to address crime in the capital after Der Spiegel published her interview comments indicating she chose not to mention a pro-Palestinian activist by name due to fears for the safety of her family.

Skip next section Our coverage of Germany's Gen Z protests

Our coverage of Germany's Gen Z protests

We've been busy covering Gen Z protests in Germany in a separate blog.

The demonstrations were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports switched to instances of violence and rioting in some cities, especially Frankfurt and Cologne, as night fell.

Follow the latest here.

Skip next section Young Germans take to the streets

Young Germans take to the streets

Youth protests have begun in cities across Germany, with demonstrators demanding better-funded schools, action on living costs and stronger climate protection. They also oppose a possible return to military conscription.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Cologne's tiny crossing barrier has a bigger future

Cologne's tiny crossing barrier has a bigger future

A railway crossing barrier just 46 centimeters (18 inches) long has become an unlikely selfie attraction in Cologne — but the city's transport operator says it serves a purpose.

The miniature arm stands beside tracks leading to a tram maintenance depot in the Weidenpesch district. It has even appeared on Google Maps as "Germany's smallest barrier."

Despite online mockery, it is no mistake. "It serves as a placeholder," said Cologne transport operator KVB spokesman Stephan Anemüller.

Installed in 2020, the barrier is to be extended once a planned cycle path is built alongside a nearby housing development. That avoids having to overhaul the crossing equipment later.

KVB is enjoying the attention. Anemüller called it "an amusing attraction" and said the operator would try to secure it a place in Cologne's city museum when it is eventually removed.

Skip next section Merkel calls for Germany's first female president

Merkel calls for Germany's first female president

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.

Everyone should ask "whether it might finally be time," Merkel told MagentaTV.

She said she knew women capable of doing the job but declined to name anyone.

The Federal Convention elects Germany's next head of state on January 30. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term. The presidency is mostly a ceremonial role.

Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner has the backing of Markus Söder, leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).

Other names being discussed include Bundestag president Julia Klockner, Education Minister Karin Prien and former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, all from Merkel's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Merkel described the debate as "strange" and criticized its "unpleasant undertone."

She also challenged her party's direction, saying the CDU's identity went beyond economic policy. "The CDU was always about building bridges to all parts of society — and that must be brought back to the forefront."

Skip next section Berlin's Left Party weighs coalition talks under tight security

Berlin's Left Party weighs coalition talks under tight security

Berlin's socialist Left Party is expected to approve coalition negotiations with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and environmentalist Greens, potentially paving the way for the city's first Left Party mayor.

The SPD and Greens have already backed talks, which could begin on Monday. But the Left Party's youth wing opposes the alliance, calling instead for a "strong socialist opposition."

Delegates gathered under tight security in Berlin's Lichtenberg district following calls for protests accusing the party of betraying voters. Its candidate for mayor, Elif Eralp, has been given personal protection.

The Left Party won September's election with 25.7% of the vote. The governing coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and SPD lost its majority.

If the three parties reach a deal, Eralp, currently the Left Party's parliamentary leader in Berlin, could become the city's next governing mayor.

entries.title: Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
entries.summary: Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. But new developments in biotech and AI are a cause for concern. DW addresses some of the most important questions about their history, risks, and control.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease

November 1, 2026

Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. But new developments in biotech and AI are a cause for concern. DW addresses some of the most important questions about their history, risks, and control.

Artificial intelligence could potentially be misused to develop biological weapons. This may sound like science fiction, but scientists, security services, and international organizations are all looking at how to deal with this scenario.

Pathogens can be analyzed and altered with ever greater precision thanks to ongoing developments in biotechnology. Meanwhile, AI is able to evaluate vast quantities of data at astonishing speeds. As a result, experts are warning that, in the long term, modern technologies could also be misused to develop biological weapons.

Security services are concerned. In October 2026, Ken McCallum, head of the British domestic intelligence service MI5, warned that artificial intelligence could increase the risk from existing, or new, biological weapons – including from non-state actors.

Fine line between valid research and misuse

A report by the American AI company Anthropic in September 2026 highlights the topicality of the debate. Anthropic said it had identified and blocked numerous attempts to use its AI assistant Claude in connection with possible biological weapon research. The report said these attempts included grant applications for so-called "gain-of-function" research, as well as projects to research avian influenza variants that were potentially the most transmissible to mammals.

At the same time, Anthropic stressed that, although it could have a military application, such research could also relate to medical prevention. The difficulty in distinguishing between legitimate science and its possible misuse is one of the biggest problems in terms of the control of modern biotechnologies.

What are biological weapons?

Concerns about biological weapons are by no means new. Many pathogens — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and certain biological toxins — have the potential for weaponization. Familiar diseases include plague, smallpox, and botulinum toxin, but anthrax is one of the most notorious biological agents. Its resistant spores can survive a long time in the environment, and it has also been the focus of research by state biological weapons programs.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs define a biological weapon as the targeted release of such biological substances for the purpose of injuring people, animals, or plants.

A biological weapon usually has two components: The biological substance itself, and a system for disseminating it. Experts refer to these as the "agent," such as a virus or bacterium, and the "delivery mechanism." Examples of the latter include missiles, spraying systems, and contaminated food.

Biological weapons belong to the so-called ABC weapons, alongside atomic (nuclear) and chemical weapons. They are often also counted as weapons of mass destruction.

How do they differ from chemical weapons?

Biological and chemical weapons differ in their mode of operation. Chemical weapons injure people through the toxic effects of chemical substances such as sarin or mustard gas. They will often take effect within minutes, or even seconds. Examples of the use of chemical weapons are the gas attacks in World War I, which involved chlorine gas, and later mustard gas; and the deployment of the nerve gas sarin in the Syrian civil war and by Saddam Hussein in Iraq.

Biological weapons, on the other hand, cause infectious disease. The effects become apparent only hours, days, or even weeks after they have been deployed. Some pathogens are also capable of spreading from person to person, meaning that the outcome is difficult to predict.

To summarize: Chemical weapons kill or injure through immediate toxicity, whereas biological weapons cause diseases. The possibility of human-to-human transmission makes the effect of a biological weapon particularly hard to calculate.

Are biological weapons subject to a worldwide ban?

Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. The first Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) came into force in 1975. This prohibits the development, stockpiling, acquisition, retention, production, and transfer of biological and toxin-based weapons.

The Convention, which has been ratified by 189 countries, can be seen as a development of the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use of biological weapons as a method of warfare. Only a few countries have not signed the agreement, or have signed but not ratified it, including Israel, Egypt, and Syria. All those who have acceded to the Convention have also committed themselves to destroying all stocks, production sites, and means of conveyance.

Chemical weapons are also internationally banned, but their control is seen as much more highly developed. The Chemical Weapons Convention is implemented by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), which can carry out inspections and oversee the destruction of chemical weapons stocks.

There is still no comparable system for controlling biological weapons. States fear that inspection could expose sensitive research data pertaining to medicine, biotechnology, or the pharmaceutical industry. This is why the control of biological weapons relies to a great extent on transparency, voluntary reporting, and good faith.

One of the best-known examples of why the ban on biological weapons is insufficient on its own to prevent their use occurred in the United States in 2001. A few weeks after the attacks of September 11, several people received letters containing anthrax spores. 22 were infected, and five died.

Why are biological weapons so hard to expose and control?

Finding biological weapons programs is much harder than controlling the production of nuclear or chemical weapons. Many technologies that could be used to develop biological weapons also have civilian applications. The same laboratory equipment used to develop vaccines and medicines could, in theory, also be used for military research.

Experts refer to this as the problem of dual use. Research can be done for peaceful medical purposes and, at the same time, have a military application.

Furthermore, a biological attack can initially look like a natural outbreak of disease. It is often only possible after extensive investigation to establish whether a pathogen was deliberately released or occurred naturally.

Perhaps that is also why biological weapons have been deployed at various times throughout history. Historical reports range from the poisoning of wells to catapulting the corpses of plague victims over the walls of a besieged town. The effectiveness of these methods is, however, disputed.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto
entries.summary: Clashes broke out as officers again dispersed housing protesters from tent camps in Lisbon and Porto. Portuguese police have repeatedly cleared tent camps erected across both cities in recent weeks.
entries.content:
November 1, 2026

Clashes broke out as officers again dispersed housing protesters from tent camps in Lisbon and Porto. Portuguese police have repeatedly cleared tent camps erected across both cities in recent weeks.

Police on Sunday cleared out protest camps in Portugal's capital, Lisbon, and Porto after thousands of housing protesters marched against a rental bill.

Around 4:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT), ‌dozens of officers moved in to dismantle camps in Lisbon's Rossio Square and Porto's Dom Joao I Square, where participants had set up tents following peaceful marches against soaring housing costs on Saturday.

Police used shields and batons to disperse protesters, and said some of the demonstrators threw bottles and paint at officers as they stormed the camps.

Police arrest 13 in Lisbon, Porto

Six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse, according to a police statement. It said 13 police were injured as they tried to take down the camps, with eight taken to hospital.

The statement also said an unspecified number of civilians were also injured.

Meanwhile, one of the lawyers representing those detained in Porto said the police response was disproportionate, arguing that both the size of the operation and the actions were excessive.

Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment.

It called a fresh rally against the police operation in the capital on Sunday afternoon. "We will not be silenced," the group said in a statement posted on social media.

Portugal's housing crisis

Hours before the eviction, more than 1,000 people marched through central Lisbon to protest against Portugal's deepening housing crisis.

Demonstrators are calling for the country's minority center-right government to scrap plans that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases.

Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill, though he has acknowledged that modifications could be made before the final vote.

Portugal is facing one of Europe's most severe housing crises, with house prices more than doubling since 2017.

entries.title: India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions
entries.summary: Thousands are expected to take part in the Indian opposition's planned mega march in New Delhi over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
entries.content:
India

India opposition holds major rally against voter roll revisions

Published November 1, 2026last updated November 1, 2026

Thousands are expected to take part in the Indian opposition's planned mega march in New Delhi over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is closed. Here is our coverage from India on Sunday, November 1:

  • India's opposition parties are marching to Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi to seek the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation
  • Rahul Gandhi tells protesters that India's election chief 'will go to jail'
  • Pollution curbs have kicked-in in the Indian capital

Skip next section Thank you for reading!

Thank you for reading!

That's all for today. We will be back with more news from India tomorrow.

Skip next section Rahul Gandhi says India's election chief 'will go to jail'

Rahul Gandhi says India's election chief 'will go to jail'

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would be removed from office and jailed, accusing him of facilitating electoral fraud.

Speaking at a rally organized by the opposition INDIA alliance in New Delhi, Gandhi alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah owed their positions to Kumar.

"Gyanesh Kumar will be removed from the post of Chief Election Commissioner. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail," Gandhi told supporters.

The Congress leader also accused authorities of manipulating elections through electronic voting machines and changes to electoral rolls.

"For years, vote theft has been happening in this country," Gandhi said, citing several state elections and the 2024 parliamentary vote.

He further claimed that 15% of India's voters had been removed from electoral rolls following the 2024 election. The allegations have not been independently verified.

Gandhi also criticized economic inequality and the treatment of farmers, young people and workers.

"The farmer is not getting his rights. The youth are not getting employment. The laborer is not getting his rights, and the entire wealth has gone into the hands of two or three people," he said.

Skip next section Home Minister Amit Shah denounces opposition rally

Home Minister Amit Shah denounces opposition rally

Union Home Minister Amit Shah took aim at opposition leader Rahul Gandhi from an event in Punjab state's Chandigarh on Sunday as the opposition alliance reached Ramlila Maidan for its rally.

He slammed the Congress for calling the opposition rally on the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, which Shah said were "incited" by the main opposition party,

"Our party held a press conference requesting that they not hold the event on November 1, 2, 3 — the very days the anti-Sikh riots took place — as it would deeply hurt the sentiments of the Sikh community, including mothers, sisters, and children. But they remained adamant," Shah said.

The senior minister of the Modi government highlighted that he was speaking from Punjab, which he went on to say was the "land of the (Sikh) Gurus."

"I strongly condemn this vile attempt. India and Punjab will never be able to forget this," he said, referring to the opposition rally.

Congress and the opposition have accused Shah and Modi of "vote theft" amid allegations of electoral irregularities.

On Saturday, Shah challenged Gandhi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav to discuss the "vote theft" row in a special session of the parliament. He has accused the opposition of evading parliamentary debate and making baseless allegations against India's poll body.

Skip next section INDIA bloc leaders arrive at Ramlila Maidan

INDIA bloc leaders arrive at Ramlila Maidan

India's opposition leaders, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, have reached Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi — the ground-zero of their rally against a sweeping review of voter lists and their demand for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

The rally is November's first public display of dissent, following near-daily protests in October by opposition parties, India's 'Cockroach' movement, student organizations and civil society groups over the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls in the world's largest democracy.

Gandhi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's political arch-rival, rode through an almost 1.5 kilometer-long (0.9 mile-long) stretch in New Delhi in an open-top jeep, with leaders of India's opposition parties seated behind him.

Thousands of people, including supporters and cadres of the opposition from different states, began gathering at Ramlila Maidan from Sunday morning, waving the national flag and party flags as they awaited the arrival of the opposition convoy.

Visuals on Indian news channels showed the opposition leaders taking their seats on a stage set up at the historic square.

Gandhi is expected to address the rally shortly.

Skip next section Opposition leaders set off for Ramlila Maidan

Opposition leaders set off for Ramlila Maidan

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has shared visuals of the opposition INDIA alliance's rally headed toward Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi.

A split screen showed a large crowd of supporters gathered at the rally site as promient opposition lawmakers seated onboard an open-top vehicle made their way to the Ramlila Maidan through Delhi's roads.

"Come to Connaught Place, let's march together. Or meet directly at Ramlila Maidan - but you must come," Gandhi wrote on X earlier at noon local time as he called for the march to "Save the Vote, Save the Nation."

Skip next section Delhi enforces winter pollution plan

Delhi enforces winter pollution plan

With winter on the horizon in New Delhi, dread of the annual smog that season brings with it has also set in. 

Starting today, the Indian capital is imposing strict and sweeping pollution curbs to tackle the toxic winter smog.

The restrictions include a ban on older vehicles registered outside the city, a suspension of dust-generating demolition activities and outdoor civil construction activities, doubling of parking fees to discourage the use of private vehicles and reduction of physical attendance in government and private-sector offices to 50%.

Agencies including the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, the Municipal Corporation, the city's transport department and traffic police have been tasked with ensuring a stringent enforcement of the winter pollution rules.

The measures will be implemeted for varying time frames, with some lasting until February 28.

"Delhi's Winter Action Plan 2026-27 comes into effect with stricter pollution controls, stronger enforcement and 24×7 monitoring. We humbly request all Delhiites to follow the guidelines and contribute towards making Delhi's air cleaner and healthier," Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta's office said.

Skip next section How has Modi's BJP reacted to the opposition stir?

How has Modi's BJP reacted to the opposition stir?

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Narendra Modi is staging a rally of its own in New Delhi, setting the stage for a battle of marches.

The BJP march will take place in West Delhi in remembrance of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, with the ruling party accusing the Congress of staging a political rally on the anniversary of the violence.

The deadly riots took place following the assassination of the then prime minister, Congress'Indira Gandhi— opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's paternal grandmother — by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984.

"The sobs of the 1984 riot victims cannot be drowned out by the noise of rallies!" the BJP wrote on X.

"The wounds of 1984 are still raw today. Congress cannot bury them under the din of its theatrics!" the party added.

The BJP also shared videos from different states in the country of rallies held over the weekend under its campaign named "Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy" to counter the Congress and the opposition.

The BJP deems the opposition protests over alleged voter roll manipulations as attempts to "create anarchy."

Skip next section INDIA bloc holds big rally against electoral irregularities, election chief

INDIA bloc holds big rally against electoral irregularities, election chief

India's political opposition is carrying out a major march in New Delhi to protest the nationwide revision of electoral rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

They are also seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The 'Chalo Dilli' march, heralded by the main opposition Congress party, will begin from Central Delhi's Connaught Place Minto Road Junction to reach Ramlila Maidan.

Top faces of the opposition alliance — called the INDIA bloc — are among those expected to participate. These include Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav and Rashtriya Janata Dal's Tejashwi Yadav.

India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which carried out its own demonstrations against Kumar last month, has also backed the opposition rally. 

What is India's electoral roll controversy?

Under a contentious nationwide voter-verification exercise, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), around 130 million names have been purged from electoral rolls.

The opposition and critics say that those struck off the voter lists include a large number of minority voters and accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. BJP denied the allegations.

The outcry against election chief Kumar began in September after an investigative report by an Indian daily said that there were divisions ​in the country's poll body — the Election Commission of India (ECI) — over the revision of voter lists, which it oversees.

Concerns emerged over the ECI's independence.

The ECI has maintained the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Opposition stages symbolic impeachment of election chief

On Saturday evening, the INDIA bloc staged a mock impeachment of the chief election commissioner. The symbolic proceedings saw opposition members reenacting a parliamentary session in a garden at Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.

"I don't think anything like this has ever happened in history. The entire opposition sitting in a garden to discuss the impeachment of the CEC, it is absurd," leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said.

He added that the opposition lawmakers had to hold the mock exercise — which even featured furniture, seating arrangements and carpeting resembling the Lok Sabha (lower house of the Indian parliament) — because they "have nowhere else to go."

"We have no other option. Every single institution ... is closed for us," Gandhi said.

Meanwhile on Sunday, the opposition expects thousands of supporters to descend upon Ramlila Maidan.

It is the first major demonstration to be held at the famous ground, located between Old and New Delhi, since it was labeled as one of the three designated protest sites in the capital last month.

Early visuals showed supporters beginning to gather at Ramlila Maidan and posters of the 'Chalo Dilli' march propped up in the capital.

The Delhi Police said that around 200 to 250 CCTV cameras have been set up at the site as part of the security arrangements.

News agency ANI reported that around 4,000 security personnel have been deployed at Ramlila Maidan.

"The organizers have set up various enclosures, and we have police personnel stationed within them. There are also pathways between these enclosures, where our police personnel are deployed to ensure the area remains secure,” deputy commissioner of police (Central District) Rohit Rajbir Singh told ANI.

The capital's traffic police announced curbs and diversions in Central Delhi ahead of the rally.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW’s studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily capsule of all the biggest headlines making a splash in India.

New Delhi has been waking up to chillier mornings, but the political heat brought on by a weekend of protests by India's bloc of opposition parties is what's gripping the capital today.

The opposition is set to hold a massive rally today at Ramlila Maidan — New Delhi's newly designated protest site — against alleged voter roll irregularities and India's top poll official.

Last evening, the opposition parties staged a mock impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as they stepped up their stir against a controversial nationwide revision of voter lists.

In other news, pollution curbs to tackle the annual winter smog in the Indian capital have come into force.

Stay with us as we bring you all this and more.

entries.title: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.
entries.content:
United States of America

Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil

November 1, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.

The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.

But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.

In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.

"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."

Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"

Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."

Good relations with Putin ally Vucic

Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.

The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.

Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.

Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.

Israel: Outcome still unclear

There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.

Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.

Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.

No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms

With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."

But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.
